steps.message:
Marguerite has the resolution-basis item open on the Ocotillo peer-review checklist and will not sign Phase 1 rev B until it closes.  I need a short note I can put in front of her that settles the resolution question on what is already on the file server, because nothing new is being run for this.

Tell me where the plume resolution index lands for the result the report rests on, with the cell size and the plume length scale behind it, and whether our band is met.  Then tell me what our resolution acceptance rests on, and whether anything about that basis needs a decision from Marguerite.

I also want to know whether the resolved-energy figure was taken inside the region the index describes, and whether the ambient values behind the plume length scale represent the site, and what the site's conditions would do to it.

Last, tell me whether the item can close, and if it cannot, what would settle it.

Put it in a Word note saved as /filesystem/CFDME-2025-041_resolution_note_revA.docx please.

Ocotillo Additive Structures — WUI Wildfire Exposure, Phase 1
Phase 1 Draft Report — Revision B (Unreviewed)
Project: CFDME-2025-041 — Ocotillo WUI Wildfire, Phase 1
Client: Ocotillo Additive Structures
Report revision: rev B (draft, unreviewed)
Prepared by: Gordon Selby, PE — AZ PE #48213
Date: 10/09/2025
1. Purpose & Scope
1.1 Purpose
This report documents the Phase 1 thermal-CFD analysis of the Ocotillo Additive Structures double-wythe printed-concrete cavity wall assembly under Sonoran Desert wildland-urban-interface exposure. The analysis is a large-eddy simulation of a fire-front segment representative of a Sonoran buffelgrass surface fire advancing on the exposed face of the assembly. The exposure envelope, fire-source characterisation, mesh study, and preliminary thermal response are reported here. Companion structural wind-pressure work under SOW Section 3.2 is documented separately.
1.2 Scope
The scope of the Phase 1 analysis is limited to:
Regime classification and selection of solver stack;
Site-envelope characterisation from Pima County ALERT ten-year hourly meteorology;
Fire-source characterisation from published Rothermel / Byram / solid-flame correlations for the specified fuel model;
Large-eddy simulation of the fire-front sub-domain at design-envelope wind speeds and directions;
Thermal treatment of the double-wythe cavity wall assembly per the project case-setup record;
Verification of the LES discretisation on the wildfire sub-domain;
Preliminary reporting of unexposed-face and tie-embedded thermal response.
1.3 Scope exclusions
Fire-resistance rating certification of the assembly is explicitly outside the scope of this report and outside the stamp boundary of The CFD ME. The certified rating for the subject wall assembly is issued separately by others (see the standard stamp block in §9). This report is a computational thermal analysis; it does not certify, extend, or modify any assembly rating.
Structural wind-pressure work per SOW §3.2 is a separate deliverable and is not included here.
2. Governing SOW Reference
2.1 Statement of Work
The governing contract for the analysis reported here is the Ocotillo Additive Structures Phase 1 Statement of Work, CFDME-2025-041, signed 10/08/2025. Two technical sections of the SOW frame the Phase 1 workscope:
2.2 SOW §3.1 — Wildfire Analysis Matrix
Six wildfire-exposure cases, formed as the cross-product of two wind directions and three wind speeds:
The two directions bracket the prevailing daytime westerly component observed at the Avra Valley WUI site; the three speeds span the site design 20-ft wind envelope of 5–12 m/s (§5).
2.3 SOW §3.2 — Structural Wind-Load Case
SOW §3.2 defines a separate structural wind-pressure extraction for the wall assembly per ASCE 7-22, sited in Tucson, Arizona, at Exposure C, Risk Category II. That extraction is reported in a separate deliverable and is not carried in this report; the SOW §3.1 wildfire matrix and the SOW §3.2 structural case are distinct workscopes and share no boundary conditions.
3. Method
3.1 Regime classification
Regime classification for this matrix follows CFD Modeling Standards — Fire & Buoyant Flows rev 4 (§2), evaluated against the site design 20-ft wind speed envelope of 5–12 m/s and the design fire heat release rate (§3.3). The classification and the resulting solver selection are documented in the project case-setup record (CFDME-2025-041_scoping_memo_20251008.docx §4) and are not re-derived here.
3.2 Solver stack
Solver stack selection for this matrix is governed by the firm modeling standard §3 and is documented in the project case-setup record; that record is the reference for the solver, inlet, combustion, and radiation model selection used to produce the results in §5 below.
3.3 Fire source
The exposed-face heat load is imposed as a sub-domain LES over a 3.0 m segment of the advancing fire front, taken at the point of nearest approach to the assembly. The total heat release rate over that segment is 30.1 MW, sourced by a volumetric heat-release term integrated over the fuel bed footprint within the sub-domain. The Byram fireline intensity and solid-flame flame length that underpin this source term are given in §5.
3.4 Wall assembly
The wall assembly is a double-wythe printed-concrete cavity wall, source of record OAS-WUI-01_revC: two 50 mm printed siliceous-aggregate concrete leaves separated by a 205 mm open-air cavity (no insulation), tied by continuous 9-gauge (3.8 mm) galvanized truss-type steel ties at 600 mm vertical spacing, 25 mm embedment each leaf. Overall assembly thickness is 305 mm. The through-wall CFD treatment selected for this assembly is documented in the project case-setup record per Modeling Standard §6.
3.5 Geometry of record
The source geometry for all cases reported here is OAS-WUI-01_revC, transmitted by the client with the signed SOW on 10/08/2025 and meshed the morning of 10/09/2025. Every case log, mesh output, and results file in this report references OAS-WUI-01_revC as source geometry. The architectural drawing for the same assembly (OAS_wall_assembly_section.png) uses the drawing-side identifier OAS-WA-305mm-DW; this refers to the same physical wall assembly as the engineering geometry of record OAS-WUI-01_revC used throughout this report.
4. Assumptions & Limitations
4.1 Assumptions
Fuel model. Sonoran buffelgrass is treated as a continuous, homogeneous surface fuel bed at the fuel load and heat content given in §5. Fuel spatial heterogeneity below the sub-domain footprint is not represented.
Fire-source stationarity. The 3.0 m front segment is held stationary within the LES sub-domain; the wall assembly is at the point of nearest approach for the sampled interval. Fire-front advance across the assembly footprint is not simulated within the sub-domain.
Meteorological stationarity. Inlet wind speed and direction are stationary within each case at the values in the SOW §3.1 matrix; diurnal, gust, and synoptic-scale variability are represented only by the envelope in §5.
Cavity contents. The cavity is modelled as open air with no insulation, per the as-built assembly.
Concrete properties. Printed siliceous-aggregate concrete properties are those in the modeling standard reference table, with temperature dependence enabled; spatial variability introduced by the printing process is not represented.
Radiation participation. Concrete surfaces are treated as grey diffuse emitters at emissivity 0.9, per the radiation model selected in the project case-setup record.
4.2 Limitations
The analysis is a thermal analysis only. It does not certify fire-resistance rating, does not predict structural collapse, and does not predict spalling.
The analysis reports response to the SOW §3.1 wildfire matrix. It does not predict survival of the assembly under exposures outside that envelope.
The ASTM E119 furnace exposure is a comparative-rating exposure; a companion E119 simulation is reported under Validation (§7) for model-verification purposes only. E119 endurance is not a wildfire survival prediction.
Validation of the wildfire configuration against a wildfire-phase physical test is scheduled for the Red Butte confirmatory window on 10/27/2025 and is not reported here.
5. Results
5.1 Site design envelope
Ten-year hourly meteorology from the Pima County ALERT network at the Avra Valley WUI site establishes the design exposure envelope:
These ranges bracket the fire-season daytime conditions used for the SOW §3.1 matrix inlets.
5.2 Fire-source characterisation
For the Sonoran buffelgrass fuel model at the site design envelope:
The 5.4 m solid-flame length is the wind-tilted Byram length. It is shorter than the still-air Heskestad correlation at 30.1 MW / 3.0 m (which would predict ~11.5 m); this gap between the two correlations is not treated as a discrepancy.
5.3 Plume dynamics
The plume in every solved case exhibits a well-organised puffing signature at the plume base, with a puffing frequency of 0.87 Hz. The puffing signature is resolved in time by the transient LES; centreline temperature and velocity monitors oscillate at that frequency about their mean values, sampled over no fewer than twenty puffing cycles at t ≥ 8 s.
5.4 Thermal response — preliminary
Preliminary plume-centreline peaks on the fine grid are T_peak ≈ 1461 K and U_z,peak ≈ 12.4 m/s at the reference probe location (0.75·D* above the source top surface). Per-case unexposed-face and tie-embedded temperature histories for the six SOW §3.1 cases will be reported in Appendix B upon completion of the production LES runs (scheduled Sprint 2, 2025-10-20).
6. Verification
6.1 Three-grid study
A three-grid study was executed on the wildfire sub-domain over the OAS-WUI-01_revC geometry, following the firm's verification reporting layout. Background cell sizes and headline monitors on the plume centreline at t = 40.0 s are:
Every mesh passes the firm mesh-quality criteria (max non-orthogonality, max skewness, max aspect ratio) with "Mesh OK." returned by checkMesh on every grid. Transient time stepping per firm standard §4 applies to all three runs; puffing period is recovered on all three grids.
6.2 Grid-to-grid comparison
Grid-to-grid behaviour of the T_peak and U_z,peak monitors is non-monotonic across the three grids. The corresponding puffing-period monitor is essentially converged from the medium grid onward. The fire-source refinement zone carries two additional refinement levels above background on every grid; the ratio of refined-zone cell size to background cell size is preserved across the three cases.
6.3 Selection of reporting grid
The fine grid (background dx = 0.5 m) is retained as the reporting grid for the six SOW §3.1 wildfire cases. Detail of the underlying LES resolution figures on that grid is given in Appendix C.
7. Validation
(To be completed. Companion simulation predicts S = 131 min for the ASTM E119 exposure; validation memo forthcoming.)
8. Conclusions

Appendix A — SOW §3.1 case matrix and boundary-condition summary
Boundary-condition summary for each of the six SOW §3.1 wildfire cases (240°/270° × 5, 8, 12 m/s at 20 ft), including wind-inlet reference height, roughness length, ambient temperature, and relative humidity from the site envelope in §5.1.
Appendix B — Per-case unexposed-face and tie-embedded temperature histories
[To be populated — one figure per case upon completion of the six SOW §3.1 production LES runs, Sprint 2.]
Appendix C — Grid Resolution Detail
Source scale for the wildfire LES sub-domain and the derived plume characteristic diameter, evaluated on the fine grid: The table below reports the fluid-only LES resolution-verification study (three grids, no conjugate solid regions); the production mesh additionally resolves the wall assembly and ties described in §3.4 at the same dx = 0.5 m background, bringing the fine-grid cell count to 11,214,862 (checkMesh output, Appendix D).
D* is computed from the source heat release rate per the standard non-dimensionalisation with ρ_∞ = 1.204 kg/m³, c_p = 1005 J/(kg·K), T_∞ = 293.15 K, g = 9.81 m/s². The Pope resolved-TKE fraction is evaluated at the centreline probe (0.75·D* above the source top surface) from the ratio of resolved to (resolved + subgrid) turbulent kinetic energy over the sampled interval.
Appendix D — checkMesh outputs and case logs
Full checkMesh outputs for the three grids, archived under /Projects/CFDME-2025-041_Ocotillo_WUI/Case/verification/ and /Projects/CFDME-2025-041_Ocotillo_WUI/Case/logs/. Solver logs for the fine-grid production runs on the six SOW §3.1 wildfire cases will be added upon completion of those runs (scheduled Sprint 2, 2025-10-20).
End of draft rev B — unreviewed. Peer review, stamp, §7 completion, and §8 conclusions to follow.

Project: CFDME-2025-041 — Ocotillo WUI Wildfire, Phase 1
Client: Ocotillo Additive Structures
Report revision: rev B (draft, unreviewed)
Prepared by: Gordon Selby, PE — AZ PE #48213
Date: 10/09/2025
1. Purpose & Scope
1.1 Purpose
This report documents the Phase 1 thermal-CFD analysis of the Ocotillo Additive Structures double-wythe printed-concrete cavity wall assembly under Sonoran Desert wildland-urban-interface exposure. The analysis is a large-eddy simulation of a fire-front segment representative of a Sonoran buffelgrass surface fire advancing on the exposed face of the assembly. The exposure envelope, fire-source characterisation, mesh study, and preliminary thermal response are reported here. Companion structural wind-pressure work under SOW Section 3.2 is documented separately.
1.2 Scope
The scope of the Phase 1 analysis is limited to:
Regime classification and selection of solver stack;
Site-envelope characterisation from Pima County ALERT ten-year hourly meteorology;
Fire-source characterisation from published Rothermel / Byram / solid-flame correlations for the specified fuel model;
Large-eddy simulation of the fire-front sub-domain at design-envelope wind speeds and directions;
Thermal treatment of the double-wythe cavity wall assembly per the project case-setup record;
Verification of the LES discretisation on the wildfire sub-domain;
Preliminary reporting of unexposed-face and tie-embedded thermal response.
1.3 Scope exclusions
Fire-resistance rating certification of the assembly is explicitly outside the scope of this report and outside the stamp boundary of The CFD ME. The certified rating for the subject wall assembly is issued separately by others (see the standard stamp block in §9). This report is a computational thermal analysis; it does not certify, extend, or modify any assembly rating.
Structural wind-pressure work per SOW §3.2 is a separate deliverable and is not included here.
2. Governing SOW Reference
2.1 Statement of Work
The governing contract for the analysis reported here is the Ocotillo Additive Structures Phase 1 Statement of Work, CFDME-2025-041, signed 10/08/2025. Two technical sections of the SOW frame the Phase 1 workscope:
2.2 SOW §3.1 — Wildfire Analysis Matrix
Six wildfire-exposure cases, formed as the cross-product of two wind directions and three wind speeds:
The two directions bracket the prevailing daytime westerly component observed at the Avra Valley WUI site; the three speeds span the site design 20-ft wind envelope of 5–12 m/s (§5).
2.3 SOW §3.2 — Structural Wind-Load Case
SOW §3.2 defines a separate structural wind-pressure extraction for the wall assembly per ASCE 7-22, sited in Tucson, Arizona, at Exposure C, Risk Category II. That extraction is reported in a separate deliverable and is not carried in this report; the SOW §3.1 wildfire matrix and the SOW §3.2 structural case are distinct workscopes and share no boundary conditions.
3. Method
3.1 Regime classification
Regime classification for this matrix follows CFD Modeling Standards — Fire & Buoyant Flows rev 4 (§2), evaluated against the site design 20-ft wind speed envelope of 5–12 m/s and the design fire heat release rate (§3.3). The classification and the resulting solver selection are documented in the project case-setup record (CFDME-2025-041_scoping_memo_20251008.docx §4) and are not re-derived here.
3.2 Solver stack
Solver stack selection for this matrix is governed by the firm modeling standard §3 and is documented in the project case-setup record; that record is the reference for the solver, inlet, combustion, and radiation model selection used to produce the results in §5 below.
3.3 Fire source
The exposed-face heat load is imposed as a sub-domain LES over a 3.0 m segment of the advancing fire front, taken at the point of nearest approach to the assembly. The total heat release rate over that segment is 30.1 MW, sourced by a volumetric heat-release term integrated over the fuel bed footprint within the sub-domain. The Byram fireline intensity and solid-flame flame length that underpin this source term are given in §5.
3.4 Wall assembly
The wall assembly is a double-wythe printed-concrete cavity wall, source of record OAS-WUI-01_revC: two 50 mm printed siliceous-aggregate concrete leaves separated by a 205 mm open-air cavity (no insulation), tied by continuous 9-gauge (3.8 mm) galvanized truss-type steel ties at 600 mm vertical spacing, 25 mm embedment each leaf. Overall assembly thickness is 305 mm. The through-wall CFD treatment selected for this assembly is documented in the project case-setup record per Modeling Standard §6.
3.5 Geometry of record
The source geometry for all cases reported here is OAS-WUI-01_revC, transmitted by the client with the signed SOW on 10/08/2025 and meshed the morning of 10/09/2025. Every case log, mesh output, and results file in

1. Scope and General Principles
This procedure governs the units in which engineering quantities are computed, recorded, exchanged, and reported
at The CFD ME. It applies to every analyst and reviewer inside the firm, to every contracted CFD hour executed by
third parties on our behalf, and to every artifact — case files, logs, hand-calc worksheets, memos, and client
deliverables — that leaves any engineer's workstation.
The governing principles are three:
SI units shall be used internally throughout all analyses. Reports transmitted to clients working in US customary units
shall include a conversion table in report Section 1. Every numeric value in every artifact shall carry its unit in the
same cell or sentence — a bare number without unit is a defect.
The three principles are jointly binding. Internal SI discipline is not satisfied by a conversion applied at report time; it is
satisfied by keeping the analysis in SI from mesh generation through post-processing so that reviewers see a single
coherent unit system when they audit a case. The conversion table is not optional decoration; on projects whose
client-facing basis is US customary (ASCE 7 wind loads, ASHRAE inputs, Red Butte lab reports quoted in inches and
pounds), the table in Section 1 is the artifact the client uses to cross-read our numbers against their own, and its
absence is grounds for rejection at peer review. The unit-in-the-same-cell rule applies to spreadsheets, CSV column
headers, plot axis labels, memo text, and inline references — no exception is made for "obvious" units or for context
inherited from a section heading.

Every mesh passes the firm mesh-quality criteria (max non-orthogonality, max skewness, max aspect

1. Purpose & Scope
1.1 Purpose
This report documents the Phase 1 thermal-CFD analysis of the Ocotillo Additive Structures double-
wythe printed-concrete cavity wall assembly under Sonoran Desert wildland-urban-interface exposure.
The analysis is a large-eddy simulation of a fire-front segment representative of a Sonoran
buffelgrass surface fire advancing on the exposed face of the assembly. The exposure envelope, fire-
source characterisation, mesh study, and preliminary thermal response are reported here. Companion
structural wind-pressure work under SOW Section 3.2 is documented separately.
1.2 Scope
The scope of the Phase 1 analysis is limited to:
Regime classification and selection of solver stack;
Site-envelope characterisation from Pima County ALERT ten-year hourly meteorology;
Fire-source characterisation from published Rothermel / Byram / solid-flame correlations for the
specified fuel model;
Large-eddy simulation of the fire-front sub-domain at design-envelope wind speeds and directions;
Thermal treatment of the double-wythe cavity wall assembly per the project case-setup record;
Verification of the LES discretisation on the wildfire sub-domain;
Preliminary reporting of unexposed-face and tie-embedded thermal response.
1.3 Scope exclusions
Fire-resistance rating certification of the assembly is explicitly outside the scope of this report
and outside the stamp boundary of The CFD ME. The certified rating for the subject wall assembly is
issued separately by others (see the standard stamp block in §9). This report is a computational
thermal analysis; it does not certify, extend, or modify any assembly rating.
Structural wind-pressure work per SOW §3.2 is a separate deliverable and is not included here.
2. Governing SOW Reference
2.1 Statement of Work
The governing contract for the analysis reported here is the Ocotillo Additive Structures Phase 1
Statement of Work, CFDME-2025-041, signed 10/08/2025. Two technical sections of the SOW frame the
Phase 1 workscope:
2.2 SOW §3.1 — Wildfire Analysis Matrix
Six wildfire-exposure cases, formed as the cross-product of two wind directions and three wind
speeds:
The two directions bracket the prevailing daytime westerly component observed at the Avra Valley WUI
site; the three speeds span the site design 20-ft wind envelope of 5–12 m/s (§5).
2.3 SOW §3.2 — Structural Wind-Load Case
SOW §3.2 defines a separate structural wind-pressure extraction for the wall assembly per ASCE 7-22,
sited in Tucson, Arizona, at Exposure C, Risk Category II. That extraction is reported in a separate
deliverable and is not carried in this report; the SOW §3.1 wildfire matrix and the SOW §3.2
structural case are distinct workscopes and share no boundary conditions.
3. Method
3.1 Regime classification
Regime classification for this matrix follows CFD Modeling Standards — Fire & Buoyant Flows rev 4
(§2), evaluated against the site design 20-ft wind speed envelope of 5–12 m/s and the design fire
heat release rate (§3.3). The classification and the resulting solver selection are documented in
the project case-setup record (CFDME-2025-041_scoping_memo_20251008.docx §4) and are not re-derived
here.
3.2 Solver stack
Solver stack selection for this matrix is governed by the firm modeling standard §3 and is
documented in the project case-setup record; that record is the reference for the solver, inlet,
combustion, and radiation model selection used to produce the results in §5 below.
3.3 Fire source
The exposed-face heat load is imposed as a sub-domain LES over a 3.0 m segment of the advancing fire
front, taken at the point of nearest approach to the assembly. The total heat release rate over that
segment is 30.1 MW, sourced by a volumetric heat-release term integrated over the fuel bed footprint
within the sub-domain. The Byram fireline intensity and solid-flame flame length that underpin this
source term are given in §5.
3.4 Wall assembly
The wall assembly is a double-wythe printed-concrete cavity wall, source of record OAS-WUI-01_revC:
two 50 mm printed siliceous-aggregate concrete leaves separated by a 205 mm open-air cavity (no
insulation), tied by continuous 9-gauge (3.8 mm) galvanized truss-type steel ties at 600 mm vertical
spacing, 25 mm embedment each leaf. Overall assembly thickness is 305 mm. The through-wall CFD
treatment selected for this assembly is documented in the project case-setup record per Modeling
Standard §6.
3.5 Geometry of record
The source geometry for all cases reported here is OAS-WUI-01_revC, transmitted by the client with
the signed SOW on 10/08/2025 and meshed the morning of 10/09/2025. Every case log, mesh output, and
results file in this report references OAS-WUI-01_revC as source geometry. The architectural drawing
for the same assembly (OAS_wall_assembly_section.png) uses the drawing-side identifier OAS-WA-305mm-
DW; this refers to the same physical wall assembly as the engineering geometry of record OAS-
WUI-01_revC used throughout this report.
4. Assumptions & Limitations
4.1 Assumptions
Fuel model. Sonoran buffelgrass is treated as a continuous, homogeneous surface fuel bed at the fuel
load and heat content given in §5. Fuel spatial heterogeneity below the sub-domain footprint is not
represented.
Fire-source stationarity. The 3.0 m front segment is held stationary within the LES sub-domain; the
wall assembly is at the point of nearest approach for the sampled interval. Fire-front advance
across the assembly footprint is not simulated within the sub-domain.
Meteorological stationarity. Inlet wind speed and direction are stationary within each case at the
values in the SOW §3.1 matrix; diurnal, gust, and synoptic-scale variability are represented only by
the envelope in §5.
Cavity contents. The cavity is modelled as open air with no insulation, per the as-built assembly.
Concrete properties. Printed siliceous-aggregate concrete properties are those in the modeling
standard reference table, with temperature dependence enabled; spatial variability introduced by the
printing process is not represented.
Radiation participation. Concrete surfaces are treated as grey diffuse emitters at emissivity 0.9,
per the radiation model selected in the project case-setup record.
4.2 Limitations
The analysis is a thermal analysis only. It does not certify fire-resistance rating, does not
predict structural collapse, and does not predict spalling.
The analysis reports response to the SOW §3.1 wildfire matrix. It does not predict survival of the
assembly under exposures outside that envelope.
The ASTM E119 furnace exposure is a comparative-rating exposure; a companion E119 simulation is
reported under Validation (§7) for model-verification purposes only. E119 endurance is not a
wildfire survival prediction.
Validation of the wildfire configuration against a wildfire-phase physical test is scheduled for the
Red Butte confirmatory window on 10/27/2025 and is not reported here.
5. Results
5.1 Site design envelope
Ten-year hourly meteorology from the Pima County ALERT network at the Avra Valley WUI site
establishes the design exposure envelope:
These ranges bracket the fire-season daytime conditions used for the SOW §3.1 matrix inlets.
5.2 Fire-source characterisation
For the Sonoran buffelgrass fuel model at the site design envelope:
The 5.4 m solid-flame length is the wind-tilted Byram length. It is shorter than the still-air
Heskestad correlation at 30.1 MW / 3.0 m (which would predict ~11.5 m); this gap between the two
correlations is not treated as a discrepancy.
5.3 Plume dynamics
The plume in every solved case exhibits a well-organised puffing signature at the plume base, with a
puffing frequency of 0.87 Hz. The puffing signature is resolved in time by the transient LES;
centreline temperature and velocity monitors oscillate at that frequency about their mean values,
sampled over no fewer than twenty puffing cycles at t ≥ 8 s.
5.4 Thermal response — preliminary
Preliminary plume-centreline peaks on the fine grid are T_peak ≈ 1461 K and U_z,peak ≈ 12.4 m/s at
the reference probe location (0.75·D* above the source top surface). Per-case unexposed-face and
tie-embedded temperature histories for the six SOW §3.1 cases will be reported in Appendix B upon
completion of the production LES runs (scheduled Sprint 2, 2025-10-20).
6. Verification
6.1 Three-grid study
A three-grid study was executed on the wildfire sub-domain over the OAS-WUI-01_revC geometry,
following the firm's verification reporting layout. Background cell sizes and headline monitors on
the plume centreline at t = 40.0 s are:
Every mesh passes the firm mesh-quality criteria (max non-orthogonality, max skewness, max aspect
ratio) with "Mesh OK." returned by checkMesh on every grid. Transient time stepping per firm
standard §4 applies to all three runs; puffing period is recovered on all three grids.
6.2 Grid-to-grid comparison
Grid-to-grid behaviour of the T_peak and U_z,peak monitors is non-monotonic across the three grids.
The corresponding puffing-period monitor is essentially converged from the medium grid onward. The
fire-source refinement zone carries two additional refinement levels above background on every grid;
the ratio of refined-zone cell size to background cell size is preserved across the three cases.
6.3 Selection of reporting grid
The fine grid (background dx = 0.5 m) is retained as the reporting grid for the six SOW §3.1

deliverable due 10/20/2025 — trace their source-term, regime, and geometry inputs back to
the numbers recorded here, rather than re-argue them case-by-case. Where a downstream
artifact needs the design fire heat release, the characteristic source diameter, or the
plume length scale, it shall cite this memo.
The scope of Phase 1 as procured under Section 3.1 of the SOW is six transient wildfire
cases (240 deg and 270 deg wind directions at 20-ft wind speeds of 5, 8, and 12 m/s). The
fire source term and the sub-domain sizing recorded here apply to that entire matrix; they
are not per-case parameters.

network for the Avra Valley WUI corridor west of Tucson (data pull:
site_met_avra_valley_2015-2024.csv, Section 3.1 of the SOW envelope). The following
envelope governs Phase 1:
These conditions define the site for regime classification (Section 4 below) and for the
source-term chain (Section 3 below). They are the same conditions carried into the Phase 1
report; no re-derivation is required.
3.  Fuel Model — Sonoran Buffelgrass at Site Design Conditions
The design fire source term is developed under the Rothermel spread-to-Byram intensity
chain, evaluated at the site design conditions of Section 2. The buffelgrass fuel model is
adopted per the SOW Section 2 definition (“Buffelgrass Fuel Model”). Fuel-model quantities
are:
•  Fuel load (dry):  w = 0.6 kg/m²
•  Low heat of combustion:  h = 18,600 kJ/kg
•  Rate of spread at design wind:  R = 0.9 m/s
R is the head-fire rate of spread produced by the Rothermel surface-fire spread model for
cured buffelgrass at the low-humidity, high-temperature, moderate-wind conditions of
Section 2. It is used here as the input to the Byram fireline-intensity relation; the
Rothermel-model input parameter tabulation for buffelgrass is on file with the project
data pull.
Byram’s fireline intensity is the product of the low heat of combustion, the available
fuel load per unit area, and the rate of spread:
I = h · w · R
= (18,600 kJ/kg) × (0.6 kg/m²) × (0.9 m/s)
= 10,040 kW/m
The Byram wind-tilted solid-flame length correlation gives:
L = 0.0775 · I^0.46
= 0.0775 × (10,040)^0.46
= 5.4 m
L above is the wind-tilted Byram flame length; it is not a still-air buoyant flame height
and is not comparable to Heskestad’s still-air correlation (see Section 5 for the
idealization record).

dimensional group is the Froude number formed on the characteristic source diameter of the
LES sub-domain:
Fr = u_wind / sqrt(g · D_char)
Taking D_char = 3.0 m (the LES sub-domain segment fixed in Section 5 below) and g = 9.81
m/s²:
sqrt(g · D_char) = sqrt(9.81 × 3.0) = sqrt(29.43) = 5.42 m/s
Evaluated across the site design wind envelope 5–12 m/s:
The Froude / plume-velocity ratio falls in the range ~0.9–2.2 across the entire design
envelope.

solver selection per §3 of that standard, shall be carried out and documented in the case
setup record before any case in this matrix is meshed.

matrix; it is not re-argued case-by-case within the envelope.

the characteristic source width used for the plume model, and the value of D_char used in
the Section 4 Froude computation and in the plume-length-scale computation below.

verification standards is an axisymmetric-source property (kW total). The two quantities

specific conversion factor between them for this project: it defines how much fire-front

Design fire heat release rate for the sub-domain:
Q = I × L_segment
= (10,040 kW/m) × (3.0 m)
= 30,120 kW
= 30.1 MW

diameter source, gives roughly 11.5 m. The 5.4 m vs 11.5 m gap between the two

quantity.

D* = ( Q / ( rho_inf · c_p · T_inf · sqrt(g) ) )^(2/5)
= ( 30,100 / ( 1.204 × 1.005 × 293.15 × 3.132 ) )^(2/5)
= ( 27.08 )^(2/5)
D* = 3.76 m.
The fine-grid cell size specified for the LES mesh study is dx = 0.5 m (the finest of the
three grids in the mesh study). This gives:
D* / dx = 3.76 / 0.5 = 7.5
which confirms the plume is adequately resolved on the fine grid. LES resolution
acceptance shall be assessed per the firm QA standard applicable to reacting-plume LES.

Interim Client Summary — Structural Wind-Load Case
1. Purpose
This DRAFT is the interim client summary of the ASCE 7-22 structural wind-load extraction
called out under SOW Section 3.2, and covers the pressure rollup produced from the wall-
probe extraction run on 10/09/2025. The scope is limited to the standalone structural
wind-load case; the Section 3.1 wildfire matrix is handled separately and is not addressed
here.
Section 3.2 asks the firm to develop the code-basis wall pressures at the OAS-WUI-01
envelope for a discrete-wind-speed check independent of the wildfire matrix, and to report
peak pressures on windward, side, and leeward faces at probe locations laid out in the
case verification plan. The values summarized below are drawn directly from the interim
probe extraction (interim_wall_pressures.csv, 10/09/2025) with no post-processing beyond
the peak rollup.
2. Case Description
Basis of loading: ASCE 7-22 (Minimum Design Loads and Associated Criteria for Buildings
and Other Structures).
Site: Tucson, Arizona (Ocotillo pilot envelope, OAS-WUI-01_revC geometry of record).
Basic wind speed, V: 96 mph (Risk Category II mapped value for the Tucson site).
Exposure category: C (open terrain with scattered obstructions, consistent with the Avra
Valley WUI setting).
Risk category: II.
Mean roof height, h: 6.4 m.
Directionality and topography factors and the velocity-pressure exposure coefficient are
applied per ASCE 7-22 Chapter 26 at the mean roof height; wall pressure coefficients on
windward, side, and leeward faces are taken from Chapter 27 (directional procedure,
enclosed low-rise building) at the site aspect ratio.
The probe grid used for peak extraction consists of ten windward probes spanning the
windward face, five probes on each side wall (north and south), and five probes on the
leeward face. Probe elevations are 0.8 m, 3.2 m, and 5.6 m above grade. All probe values
reported are peak (envelope) values from the interim extraction.
3. Results
The table below reproduces the peak pressures from the interim extraction file exactly as
recorded.
Sign convention: positive pressures act inward on the wall face; negative pressures
indicate suction (outward). Values are peaks across the interim probe set; the full per-
probe listing is retained in interim_wall_pressures.csv.
4. Discussion
Taken at face value, the pressures returned by the interim rollup are negligible relative
to the structural design demand envelope typically associated with the framing of a 6.4 m
mean-roof-height enclosed building at a 96 mph basic wind speed in Exposure C. A 12.4 Pa
peak windward pressure is a very small fraction of the wall loads that would ordinarily
drive sizing of tie, header, and out-of-plane bending checks for a printed-concrete
assembly of this scale, and the corresponding side-wall and leeward suctions (−9.5 Pa and
−6.1 Pa peak) are similarly small.
On that basis the interim reading is that the ASCE 7-22 wall loading, taken as extracted,
does not govern the OAS-WUI-01 envelope. Wildfire-driven radiative and convective loading
(SOW Section 3.1) and the E119 fire-endurance envelope remain the controlling design
considerations for the assembly. No structural remediation of the OAS-WUI-01_revC envelope
is indicated by this interim result.
The client should treat these figures as provisional pending peer review under the firm's
QA workflow. The values here are unchanged from the interim rollup and have not been
checked against boundary-condition inputs or reconciled with the ASCE 7-22 velocity-
pressure and pressure-coefficient hand calculation feeding the extraction; those cross-
checks are open items on the peer-review checklist and will be addressed before the Phase
1 structural wind-load memo is issued.

adopted per the SOW Section 2 definition (“Buffelgrass Fuel Model”). Fuel-model quantities
are:
•  Fuel load (dry):  w = 0.6 kg/m²
•  Low heat of combustion:  h = 18,600 kJ/kg
•  Rate of spread at design wind:  R = 0.9 m/s
R is the head-fire rate of spread produced by the Rothermel surface-fire spread model for
cured buffelgrass at the low-humidity, high-temperature, moderate-wind conditions of
Section 2. It is used here as the input to the Byram fireline-intensity relation; the
Rothermel-model input parameter tabulation for buffelgrass is on file with the project
data pull.
Byram’s fireline intensity is the product of the low heat of combustion, the available
fuel load per unit area, and the rate of spread:
I = h · w · R
= (18,600 kJ/kg) × (0.6 kg/m²) × (0.9 m/s)
= 10,040 kW/m
The Byram wind-tilted solid-flame length correlation gives:
L = 0.0775 · I^0.46
= 0.0775 × (10,040)^0.46
= 5.4 m
L above is the wind-tilted Byram flame length; it is not a still-air buoyant flame height
and is not comparable to Heskestad’s still-air correlation (see Section 5 for the
idealization record).
4.  Froude / Regime Assessment
Regime selection follows CFDME_Modeling_Standards_Fire_rev4.pdf §2. The controlling non-
dimensional group is the Froude number formed on the characteristic source diameter of the
LES sub-domain:
Fr = u_wind / sqrt(g · D_char)
Taking D_char = 3.0 m (the LES sub-domain segment fixed in Section 5 below) and g = 9.81
m/s²:
sqrt(g · D_char) = sqrt(9.81 × 3.0) = sqrt(29.43) = 5.42 m/s
Evaluated across the site design wind envelope 5–12 m/s:
The Froude / plume-velocity ratio falls in the range ~0.9–2.2 across the entire design
envelope.
Regime classification.  Classification against the Modeling Standard §2 thresholds, and
solver selection per §3 of that standard, shall be carried out and documented in the case
setup record before any case in this matrix is meshed.
This classification is made once, at the firm level, for the entire Phase 1 wildfire
matrix; it is not re-argued case-by-case within the envelope.
5.  LES Sub-Domain
The LES sub-domain represents a 3.0 m segment of the flaming front. This segment length is
the characteristic source width used for the plume model, and the value of D_char used in
the Section 4 Froude computation and in the plume-length-scale computation below.
5.1  Line vs Axisymmetric Reconciliation
The Byram fireline-intensity relation of Section 3 gives an intensity per unit length of
the fire front (kW/m). The plume length scale D* referred to by the firm modeling and
verification standards is an axisymmetric-source property (kW total). The two quantities
are not interchangeable and cannot be composed directly. The 3.0 m segment length is the
specific conversion factor between them for this project: it defines how much fire-front
length is captured within one LES sub-domain, and therefore what total heat release rate
the plume model sees.
Design fire heat release rate for the sub-domain:
Q = I × L_segment
= (10,040 kW/m) × (3.0 m)
= 30,120 kW
= 30.1 MW

•  Flame depth and flame residence time are not resolved in this sub-domain. The flaming
front is represented as an equivalent 3.0 m characteristic-diameter source patch.
•  The wind-tilted Byram flame length L = 5.4 m from Section 3 is a wind-tilted
correlation length; it is not a still-air buoyant flame height. Heskestad’s still-air
flame-heigh
[... 470 characters cut ...]
)
= ( 30,100 / ( 1.204 × 1.005 × 293.15 × 3.132 ) )^(2/5)
= ( 27.08 )^(2/5)
D* = 3.76 m.
The fine-grid cell size specified for the LES mesh study is dx = 0.5 m (the finest of the
three grids in the mesh study). This gives:
D* / dx = 3.76 / 0.5 = 7.5
which confirms the plume is adequately resolved on the fine grid. LES resolution
acceptance shall be assessed per the firm QA standard applicable to reacting-plume LES.
6.  Wall Assembly Note
The through-wall response of the assembly cannot be modelled as heat conduction through a
single solid slab. Per the OAS-WUI-01_revC wall assembly section
(Geometry/OAS_wall_assembly_section.png), the assembly is a double-wythe cavity system:
two 50 mm printed-concrete leaves separated by a 205 mm open-air cavity (overall thickness
305 mm), tied together by continuous 9-gauge (3.8 mm) galvanized truss-type steel ties
spaced 600 mm on centre vertically, embedded 25 mm into each leaf. The cavity carries no
insulation. The architectural drawing (OAS_wall_assembly_section.png) uses the drawing-
side identifier OAS-WA-305mm-DW in its title block; this refers to the same physical wall
assembly as the engineering geometry of record OAS-WUI-01_revC used throughout the SOW,
this memo, and all downstream analysis artifacts.
The metallic ties are a continuous parallel thermal path between the exposed and unexposed
leaves; their conductivity (~45 W/m·K) is more than an order of magnitude above the
siliceous-aggregate concrete of the leaves, and they are the reason the single-point
criterion governs over the average-rise criterion in the ASTM E119 test result of record.
Per CFDME_Modeling_Standards_Fire_rev4.pdf §6, the through-wall modeling treatment for
this assembly shall be selected and documented in the case setup record before meshing,
accounting for the metallic ties’ thermal-bridge role identified above. Temperature-
dependent solid properties (k, ρ, c_p) apply per Modeling Standard §3.5.

THE CFD ME | Tucson, Arizona | CFD Modeling Standards — Fire & Buoyant Flows | rev 4 |
Effective 08/15/2025
Document: CFDME_Modeling_Standards_Fire_rev4 Author of record: Marguerite Falk, PE — Technical
Director &
Reviewing Engineer Registration: Arizona PE #42798 Supersedes: rev 3 (effective 02/01/2024)
Distribution:
Firm-internal. All engineers and contracted CFD personnel performing fire, plume, wildfire,
cavity-wall, or
buoyant-flow work under the CFD ME name.
1. Purpose & Scope
This standard is the firm-internal governing document for every CFD analysis undertaken by The
CFD ME that
involves combustion, fire-driven buoyancy, wildland or WUI fire behaviour, compartment fires,
plume dispersion from
thermal sources, or conjugate heat transfer through fire-exposed building assemblies. It
applies to work performed by
employees of the firm, by remote engineers under a CFD ME employment agreement, and to any CFD
hours
procured from an outside laboratory or contract shop. Where a subcontracted case is delivered
against a CFDME
project number, the deliverable is expected to conform to this standard on receipt; deviations
must be identified in the
transmittal and corrected before the case enters the firm's verification queue.
The standard is normative. Sections use "shall" and "must" for mandatory provisions, "should"
for recommended
practice, and "may" for permitted alternatives. Where this document differs from a general-
purpose CFD reference or
from a client-supplied specification, this document governs firm work product; a client-driven
deviation shall be
captured in writing under the change-order provisions of the applicable Statement of Work.
The scope of this rev 4 explicitly includes:
• Open-atmosphere fire and wildfire simulations under wind loading.
• Compartment and enclosure fire simulations.
• Multi-region conjugate heat transfer through building assemblies exposed to a design fire,
including double-wythe
and cavity-wall constructions.
• Verification of mesh and time-step resolution for large-eddy simulations (LES) of buoyant
reacting flow.
• Validation of firm predictions against certified third-party fire-endurance testing.
The scope explicitly excludes non-reacting external aerodynamics, forced-ventilation HVAC
problems below the
combustion threshold, and high-altitude compressible aerodynamics. Those regimes are governed
by separate firm
standards and are called out in Section 7 of this document.
2. Regime Selection
Fire problems shall be classified by the ratio of the incident wind velocity to the buoyancy-
driven plume velocity scale
before any solver is selected. The controlling non-dimensional group is the Froude number
formed on the
characteristic fire diameter:
Fr = u_wind / sqrt(g·D)
where u_wind is the design wind speed at plume height, g is gravitational acceleration, and D
is the
characteristic fire diameter (for a distributed source, the equivalent-area diameter of the LES
sub-domain segment).
Three regimes are recognised:
1. Buoyancy-dominated (still-air) plume — Fr much less than 1. The plume rises vertically; wind
is negligible.
This regime admits a still-air buoyant treatment. 2. Mixed convection - Fr of order one, i.e.
u_wind
~ sqrt(g·D). Wind and buoyancy contribute comparable momentum. The plume tilts, entrainment is
asymmetric,
and the puffing structure interacts with the incoming boundary layer. This regime must be
solved as a wind-forced,
buoyancy-reacting problem using the full fire solver package of Section 3. Substituting a
still-air buoyant plume
when wind is present is prohibited under this standard, regardless of how "small" the wind
appears in comparison to
the flame length. 3. Momentum-dominated — Fr much greater than 1. Wind dominates. Buoyancy
still matters for
flame tilt and for near-source combustion but the far-field plume behaves as a passive scalar
in a shear flow.
The regime call shall be made and recorded in the case setup memo at project kickoff. For the
firm's Sonoran Desert
WUI design envelope (20-ft winds of 5–12 m/s over fire diameters of order a few metres), the
ratio is order one and
the regime is mixed convection; this call has been made once at the firm level and shall not be
re-argued
case-by-case within that envelope.
Where the site meteorology or fuel model places a case outside the envelope for which a regime
call already exists,
the responsible engineer shall compute Fr, record the value in the setup memo, and select the
regime from the
classification above. Reviewers shall reject any case in which the regime is not identified in
writing before the solver is
chosen.
3. Fire Solver Package
For all cases in the mixed-convection or buoyancy-dominated regimes with combustion present,
the firm shall use the
fireFoam solver family: a reacting, buoyant, low-Mach, large-eddy simulation solver derived
from the OpenFOAM
reacting-flow codebase. rev 4 mandates the following solver stack and configuration.
3.1 Solver. The solver is fireFoam. It shall be built against the firm's supported OpenFOAM
version and pulled from
the firm reference-case library rather than assembled from external sources at case start.
3.2 Wind inlet. The atmospheric wind boundary shall use atmBoundaryLayerInletVelocity with the
site
roughness length, reference height, and reference velocity taken from the project's site
meteorological pull. The
companion turbulence quantities (k, epsilon or omega as applicable to the SGS closure) shall
use their matching
atmBoundaryLayer* boundary conditions so that the inlet profile is thermodynamically and
turbulently
self-consistent. Uniform-velocity inlets, plug flow, or synthetic-turbulence generators bolted
onto a uniform inlet shall
not be used for open-atmosphere fire cases.
3.3 Combustion model. The combustion closure shall be EDC combustion — the Eddy Dissipation
Concept, in the
finite-rate variant that couples the mean chemistry to the sub-grid strain-rate. Infinitely-
fast Arrhenius,
mixture-fraction-only, and non-reacting passive-scalar surrogates for the fire shall not be
substituted.
3.4 Radiation model. The radiation closure shall be fvDOM, the finite-volume Discrete Ordinates
Method, with the
number of angular directions and the wavelength banding chosen from the firm reference table
for the fuel and flame
temperature range. The absorption/emission coefficients for participating media shall be set
consistent with the
combustion product composition, not defaulted. Simple radiation models (P1, view-factor) shall
not substitute for
fvDOM in cases where cavity or enclosure radiation participates in the heat balance.
3.5 Thermophysical properties. Fluid-region properties (species, transport, thermo) shall use
the JANAF/NASA
polynomials shipped with the firm reference library. Solid-region properties (concrete, steel,
gypsum, insulation,
printed masonry, and any purpose-built assembly material) shall be temperature-dependent: k,
rho, and cp shall
each be entered as a temperature-tabulated function or a supported polynomial fit over the
design temperature
range. Constant-property short-cuts for solid regions in fire cases are not permitted.
3.6 Forbidden substitutions. rev 4 explicitly forbids substituting a steady HVAC configuration
(buoyantSimpleFoam
or any other steady RANS buoyant solver) for the fireFoam package in any case in scope of this
standard. The
steady HVAC solver family is validated for interior building airflow at metre-per-second-scale
velocities without
combustion or radiation; it is not a permissible starting point for fire work.
4. Transient Behaviour and Time-Step Control
Buoyant fire plumes are not stationary flows. The plume necks, sheds, and re-forms at a
characteristic frequency that
depends only on the fire diameter and gravity. The empirical Cetegen–Ahmed relationship,
adopted by the firm as
normative for design fires in the buoyancy-dominated and mixed-convection regimes, gives the
puffing frequency as
f = 1.5 · D^(-1/2) Hz
with D in metres. This is a physical property of the plume, not a numerical artefact.
Worked example. For a firm-standard LES sub-domain segment of D = 3.0 m, the puffing frequency
is
f = 1.5 · (3.0)^(-1/2) = 0.87 Hz
corresponding to a puffing period of approximately 1.15 s. Every LES run at this diameter shall
be expected to display
monitor-point oscillation at this frequency; that oscillation is the signature of physically-
resolved plume dynamics.
No time-invariant resolution. Because the plume oscillates at a finite, deterministic, physical
frequency, no
time-invariant flow field exists that any residual-tolerance schedule can converge to.
Time-step control. Transient LES shall use adaptive time-stepping keyed to the Courant number.
The following
controlDict entries are mandatory:
• application fireFoam;
• adjustTimeStep yes;
• maxCo 0.9;
• maxDeltaT <case-specific ceiling, typically 0.01 s>;
• writeControl adjustableRunTime;
• writeInterval <chosen so that at least 25 samples per puffing period are captured on
monitors>;
The writeControl adjustableRunTime setting is required so that write intervals are pegged to
wall-clock time
in the simulation rather than to solver iteration count, which permits the puffing signal to be
sampled at a uniform rate.
Simulated end times shall span a minimum of 20 puffing periods after the initial transient has
cleared, so that
averages, spectra, and RMS quantities are formed on a statistically meaningful window. For a
3.0 m fire that is a
simulated interval of no less than approximately 23 seconds of physical time, exclusive of
startup.
5. Turbulence Modeling
The turbulence closure for cases in scope of this standard is large-eddy simulation. The sub-
grid-scale (SGS) closure
shall be either:
• Dynamic Smagorinsky — with the standard Germano–Lilly dynamic procedure and a firm-default
test-filter width
of twice the mesh spacing; or
• WALE (Wall-Adapting Local Eddy-viscosity) — preferred where solid boundaries carry a
significant fraction of
the thermal load, because WALE returns the correct near-wall scaling of the SGS viscosity
without requiring van
Driest damping.
The choice between the two shall be recorded in the case setup memo. Static Smagorinsky with a
hand-tuned
constant, k-epsilon variants applied to LES, and hybrid RANS/LES formulations are not permitted
under rev 4 for
cases in scope.
Wall functions at solid boundaries shall be the OpenFOAM standard high-Reynolds treatment
appropriate to the SGS
closure and the local y+ range. The mesh at solid walls shall be sized so that the first-cell
y+ stays within the
recommended band for the chosen wall function across the design range of the flow, and this
shall be verified after
the initial transient by inspection of the wall-shear field.
6. Multi-Region Conjugate Heat Transfer for Cavity-Wall Assemblies
Fire-exposed building assemblies in the firm's project portfolio are commonly double-wythe
(double-leaf) cavity
constructions with a solid outer leaf, an internal air cavity, and a solid inner leaf. The two
leaves are typically
connected by discrete metallic ties (galvanized-steel truss ties or comparable) at regular
vertical spacing, embedded
some distance into each leaf. These ties are a metallic thermal bridge across the assembly and,
in ASTM E119
practice, they set the single-point temperature-rise criterion.
For any such assembly under a design fire, the CFD case shall be a multi-region conjugate heat
transfer setup,
not a single-region simulation with lumped-wall boundary conditions. The following region
topology is mandatory:
1. Outer leaf — solid region. Temperature-dependent k, rho, cp per the firm concrete table.
Cell size at the
fire-exposed face fine enough to resolve the thermal boundary layer. 2. Cavity — fluid region
with participating
radiation. Air properties temperature-dependent; radiation solved with fvDOM as in Section 3;
cavity emissivities set
from the firm assembly library. 3. Inner leaf — solid region. Same treatment as the outer leaf.
4. Ties — each metallic
tie is a separate solid region, geometrically embedded through both leaves and terminating in
the cavity air. Ties are
not represented as a smeared conductivity on the leaf regions and are not omitted. Steel k,
rho, cp are
temperature-dependent over the design temperature range.
Region-to-region coupling at every solid–solid and solid–fluid interface shall use the OpenFOAM
chtMultiRegion*
coupled boundary conditions with matched temperature and heat flux across the interface.
Contact resistance at
tie-concrete embedments shall be applied when a firm-approved value is available; where no
value is available,
perfect thermal contact is the conservative default for single-point temperature-rise
prediction.
Mesh refinement. Refinement zones shall be defined at every tie–concrete interface, so that the
concentrated
conduction into the tie is captured with cell dimensions at least a factor of four finer than
the bulk leaf mesh at the
embedment. Failure to refine at tie–concrete interfaces has been observed in past casework to
underpredict the
single-point temperature rise and thereby to overpredict endurance; rev 4 mandates the
refinement to eliminate that
failure mode.
7. Cross-Regime Transfer
Validated status attaches to a case within an envelope, not to a directory. A case is validated
for the physical
regime, the boundary conditions, the fuel model, the geometry, and the solver package under
which it was verified
against a reference. Copying the case directory to a new project and changing the geometry does
not carry the
validation with the copy.
Geometry and mesh topology are regime-independent: a well-formed hexahedral mesh of a printed-
concrete wall
assembly is a well-formed mesh whether the outer boundary condition is a fire, a wind load, or
a room-air HVAC inlet.
Physics, however, is regime-dependent. When the regime changes, the following shall be rebuilt
from first principles
and not carried across:
• Freestream and inlet conditions (wind speed, direction, roughness, ambient temperature,
humidity).
• Solver selection (fireFoam vs. non-reacting solver vs. steady HVAC solver vs. compressible
aerodynamics
solver).
• Combustion model (present with EDC, absent, or substituted per Section 3).
• Radiation model (fvDOM with participating media, absent, or reduced-order).
• Turbulence closure (LES SGS choice, RANS, hybrid — per the regime call).
• Thermophysical property treatment (temperature-dependent vs. constant).
Reuse is prohibited without full physics rebuild. In particular:
• A validated non-reacting external-aerodynamics case (e.g. from prior aerospace work) shall
not be extended into
a fire case by adding a heat-release term. The compressible non-reacting envelope does not
overlap the
reacting-buoyant envelope, and the freestream density, the inlet turbulence, the solver, and
the closures all differ.
• A validated HVAC interior-building-airflow case (steady, low-velocity, no combustion, no
radiation, adiabatic
external walls) shall not be carried forward into any case in scope of this standard without a
full physics rebuild.
The HVAC envelope does not overlap the fire or plume regime; validated status in the former
regime confers no
validated status in the latter.
• A validated aerospace high-altitude compressible case shall not be pulled forward as the
physics basis for a
ground-level fire simulation.
Where a project geometry and a good mesh already exist from an earlier case in a different
regime, they may be
retained and re-used; the physics on top of them shall be built new to this standard. Case-
directory reuse without a
physics rebuild has been the root cause of firm rework in the past and rev 4 is explicit that
it is not acceptable
practice.
8. Verification and Validation
Verification (numerical correctness of the solve) and validation (agreement with physical
reference) are governed by
separate firm procedures and are not restated in full here.
• Mesh and time-step verification, LES resolution acceptance (D*/dx and Pope resolved-TKE
tests), and the scope
of applicability of Roache/Richardson grid-convergence-index methods shall follow the current
revision of the firm
QA Verification Standard — Mesh & Resolution. Engineers shall consult it before setting up any
three-grid or resolution study; the scope statement in it governs which verification methods
are permissible for
LES versus for steady RANS work.
• Validation against physical reference - the E = S - D formulation, validation uncertainty
u_val, and
the firm acceptance criterion — shall follow the current revision of the firm Validation QA
Procedure & Acceptance
Criterion, which is itself aligned with ASME V&V 20. Certified third-party test reports are the
required source
of the reference value D; it governs the treatment of client-amended data.
The verification and validation sections of any project report shall cite the current revision
numbers of both standards in
force at the time the report is issued.
9. References
• OpenFOAM Foundation, OpenFOAM User Guide, chapters covering the fireFoam solver family,
chtMultiRegionFoam conjugate heat transfer, atmBoundaryLayer* boundary conditions, and the
fvDOM
radiation model. Firm licence held; consulted for solver terminology and dictionary syntax.
• ASME V&V 20-2009, Standard for Verification and Validation in Computational Fluid Dynamics
and Heat Transfer.
Invoked through firm document the Validation Procedure.
• ASTM E119, Standard Test Methods for Fire Tests of Building Construction and Materials.
Invoked through firm
document the External Standards Digest, current revision.
• The CFD ME, QA Verification Standard — Mesh & Resolution rev 3.
• The CFD ME, Validation QA Procedure & Acceptance Criterion rev 2.
• The CFD ME, External Standards Digest , current revision.
• Cetegen, B. M., and Ahmed, T. A., Experiments on the periodic instability of buoyant plumes
and pool fires,
Combustion and Flame, source of the f = 1.5·D^(-1/2) correlation adopted in Section 4.

The turbulence closure for cases in scope of this standard is large-eddy simulation. The sub-grid-scale (SGS) closure

• Dynamic Smagorinsky — with the standard Germano–Lilly dynamic procedure and a firm-default test-filter width

the thermal load, because WALE returns the correct near-wall scaling of the SGS viscosity without requiring van
Driest damping.
The choice between the two shall be recorded in the case setup memo. Static Smagorinsky with a hand-tuned
constant, k-epsilon variants applied to LES, and hybrid RANS/LES formulations are not permitted under rev 4 for
cases in scope.
Wall functions at solid boundaries shall be the OpenFOAM standard high-Reynolds treatment appropriate to the SGS
closure and the local y+ range. The mesh at solid walls shall be sized so that the first-cell y+ stays within the
recommended band for the chosen wall function across the design range of the flow, and this shall be verified after
the initial transient by inspection of the wall-shear field.

6. Multi-Region Conjugate Heat Transfer for Cavity-Wall Assemblies
Fire-exposed building assemblies in the firm's project portfolio are commonly double-wythe (double-leaf) cavity
constructions with a solid outer leaf, an internal air cavity, and a solid inner leaf. The two leaves are typically
connected by discrete metallic ties (galvanized-steel truss ties or comparable) at regular vertical spacing, embedded
some distance into each leaf. These ties are a metallic thermal bridge across the assembly and, in ASTM E119
practice, they set the single-point temperature-rise criterion.
For any such assembly under a design fire, the CFD case shall be a multi-region conjugate heat transfer setup,
not a single-region simulation with lumped-wall boundary conditions. The following region topology is mandatory:
1. Outer leaf — solid region. Temperature-dependent k, rho, cp per the firm concrete table. Cell size at the
fire-exposed face fine enough to resolve the thermal boundary layer. 2. Cavity — fluid region with participating
radiation. Air properties temperature-dependent; radiation solved with fvDOM as in Section 3; cavity emissivities set
from the firm assembly library. 3. Inner leaf — solid region. Same treatment as the outer leaf. 4. Ties — each metallic
tie is a separate solid region, geometrically embedded through both leaves and terminating in the cavity air. Ties are
not represented as a smeared conductivity on the leaf regions and are not omitted. Steel k, rho, cp are
temperature-dependent over the design temperature range.
Region-to-region coupling at every solid–solid and solid–fluid interface shall use the OpenFOAM chtMultiRegion*
coupled boundary conditions with matched temperature and heat flux across the interface. Contact resistance at
tie-concrete embedments shall be applied when a firm-approved value is available; where no value is available,
perfect thermal contact is the conservative default for single-point temperature-rise prediction.

 Mesh refinement. Refinement zones shall be defined at every tie–concrete interface, so that the concentrated
conduction into the tie is captured with cell dimensions at least a factor of four finer than the bulk leaf mesh at the
embedment. Failure to refine at tie–concrete interfaces has been observed in past casework to underpredict the
single-point temperature rise and thereby to overpredict endurance; rev 4 mandates the refinement to eliminate that
failure mode.

7. Cross-Regime Transfer
Validated status attaches to a case within an envelope, not to a directory. A case is validated for the physical
regime, the boundary conditions, the fuel model, the geometry, and the solver package under which it was verified
against a reference. Copying the case directory to a new project and changing the geometry does not carry the
validation with the copy.
Geometry and mesh topology are regime-independent: a well-formed hexahedral mesh of a printed-concrete wall
assembly is a well-formed mesh whether the outer boundary condition is a fire, a wind load, or a room-air HVAC inlet.
Physics, however, is regime-dependent. When the regime changes, the following shall be rebuilt from first principles
and not carried across:

• Freestream and inlet conditions (wind speed, direction, roughness, ambient temperature, humidity).
• Solver selection (fireFoam vs. non-reacting solver vs. steady HVAC solver vs. compressible aerodynamics
solver).

• Combustion model (present with EDC, absent, or substituted per Section 3).
• Radiation model (fvDOM with participating media, absent, or reduced-order).
• Turbulence closure (LES SGS choice, RANS, hybrid — per the regime call).
• Thermophysical property treatment (temperature-dependent vs. constant).
Reuse is prohibited without full physics rebuild. In particular:

• A validated non-reacting external-aerodynamics case (e.g. from prior aerospace work) shall not be extended into
a fire case by adding a heat-release term. The compressible non-reacting envelope does not overlap the
reacting-buoyant envelope, and the freestream density, the inlet turbulence, the solver, and the closures all differ.

• A validated HVAC interior-building-airflow case (steady, low-velocity, no combustion, no radiation, adiabatic
external walls) shall not be carried forward into any case in scope of this standard without a full physics rebuild.
The HVAC envelope does not overlap the fire or plume regime; validated status in the former regime confers no
validated status in the latter.

• A validated aerospace high-altitude compressible case shall not be pulled forward as the physics basis for a
ground-level fire simulation.
Where a project geometry and a good mesh already exist from an earlier case in a different regime, they may be
retained and re-used; the physics on top of them shall be built new to this standard. Case-directory reuse without a
physics rebuild has been the root cause of firm rework in the past and rev 4 is explicit that it is not acceptable
practice.

8. Verification and Validation
Verification (numerical correctness of the solve) and validation (agreement with physical reference) are governed by
separate firm procedures and are not restated in full here.

• Mesh and time-step verification, LES resolution acceptance (D*/dx and Pope resolved-TKE tests), and the scope
of applicability of Roache/Richardson grid-convergence-index methods shall follow the current revision of the firm
QA Verification Standard — Mesh & Resolution. Engineers shall consult it before setting up any
three-grid or resolution study; the scope statement in it governs which verification methods are permissible for
LES versus for steady RANS work.

• Validation against physical reference - the E = S - D formulation, validation uncertainty u_val, and
the firm acceptance criterion — shall follow the current revision of the firm Validation QA Procedure & Acceptance
Criterion, which is itself aligned with ASME V&V 20. Certified third-party test reports are the required source
of the reference value D; it governs the treatment of client-amended data.

 The verification and validation sections of any project report shall cite the current revision numbers of both standards in
force at the time the report is issued.

1. Purpose & Scope
This standard establishes the firm's minimum requirements for demonstrating that a CFD result is grid-independent
(for steady Reynolds-averaged work) or adequately resolved (for large-eddy simulation), and specifies how the
underlying evidence must be presented in the Verification section of every deliverable that leaves the firm.
The standard applies to every project executed by The CFD ME staff and to every subcontracted deliverable
prepared on the firm's behalf, including work performed by Mulshi Simulation Labs and any other external contractor
operating under a CFD ME work order. Reviewing Engineer sign-off on the peer-review checklist requires explicit
confirmation that the requirements of this document have been met.
Revision 3 rewrites the LES portion of the standard. The rev 2 language treated the Roache/Richardson grid
convergence index (GCI) as the default verification instrument for every solve regardless of turbulence treatment.
Two internal audits and a client peer review in Q1 2025 established that the treatment is technically incorrect for
large-eddy simulation and produces verification evidence that will not survive third-party scrutiny. The corrected
treatment is set out in Sections 4 and 5.
Nothing in this standard modifies the firm's Validation QA Procedure & Acceptance Criterion
(Firm/QA/CFDME_Validation_Procedure_rev2), the firm's Modeling Standards for Fire & Buoyant Flows
, current revision, or the Units and Conversions SOP
(Firm/Standards/CFDME_Units_SOP_rev2). Where the requirements of this standard intersect those documents, all of them
apply concurrently.

2. Definitions
Grid convergence index (GCI). A quantitative estimator of numerical uncertainty attributable to spatial discretisation
error, computed from a monotonic sequence of solutions on systematically refined grids under an assumed observed
order of accuracy. Reported as a percentage band on a selected integrated quantity of interest. The GCI is defined
for solutions that converge to a unique grid-independent limit as the mesh is refined.
Plume resolution index (D*/dx). The ratio of the characteristic plume diameter D* to the representative fire-region
cell edge length dx. D* is the buoyancy-driven length scale associated with a fire heat release rate Q_dot and is
defined as
D* = ( Q_dot / ( rho_inf · cp · T_inf · sqrt(g) ) )^{2/5}
where rho_inf, cp and T_inf are the ambient density, specific heat and absolute temperature respectively, and g is
gravitational acceleration. The index D*/dx is the standard measure of how many cells span the buoyancy-dominated
length scale of a fire plume.
Resolved turbulent kinetic energy (k_res). The turbulent kinetic energy carried by the explicitly resolved velocity
fluctuations in a large-eddy simulation, distinct from the sub-grid-scale contribution k_sgs modelled by the closure.
The resolved fraction is defined as k_res / (k_res + k_sgs).
RANS and steady work. In this document, "RANS and steady work" means Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes
simulations run to steady state, whether solved with a pseudo-time or true-steady solver, including internal buoyant
airflow of the type in the Copperline municipal HVAC envelope. Unsteady RANS (URANS) is treated as RANS for the
purposes of Section 4.
LES. Large-eddy simulation, including the firm's reacting-fire LES stack (fireFoam with EDC combustion and fvDOM
radiation) and any non-reacting LES of atmospheric or building flow.

3. General Requirements for Verification
Every deliverable that reports a CFD result shall contain a Verification section, plainly labelled as such, appearing in
the body of the report ahead of Validation and ahead of Results. The Verification section shall state, at minimum:

 (a) The turbulence treatment used (RANS, URANS, or LES) and, for LES, the sub-grid-scale closure.
(b) The representative cell edge length dx in the region of interest, and the total cell count.
(c) The verification basis chosen from Section 4 or Section 5, together with the numerical evidence supporting that
basis.
(d) A single-sentence statement identifying which acceptance criterion has been met and by what margin.
The Verification section shall not be an appendix pointer. Numerical values that support the verification claim shall
appear in the body. Supporting figures, residual histories, and mesh-slice imagery may be relegated to an appendix
and referenced.
Verification is prerequisite to Validation. A deliverable whose Verification section is absent, incomplete, or
inconsistent with this standard shall not be released for client transmission and shall not carry a Reviewing Engineer
signature.

4. Grid Convergence Index (GCI)
The Roache/Richardson grid convergence index is the firm's verification instrument for RANS and steady work only.
GCI is not valid for LES and shall not be used to verify any large-eddy result issued from this firm.
The reason is physical. Under systematic mesh refinement, an LES does not converge to a unique grid-independent
solution. As the filter width narrows, energy migrates from the modelled sub-grid-scale contribution into the explicitly
resolved field; the resolved-to-modelled turbulence split changes with the mesh. A three-grid sequence of LES
solutions therefore records a change in the physical content of the simulation between grids rather than a
discretisation-error tail collapsing toward a limit. The Richardson extrapolation on which the GCI is built assumes that
limit exists. It does not exist for LES, and therefore GCI values computed from an LES three-grid study are
numerically well-formed but physically meaningless. Non-monotonic behaviour in an LES three-grid quantity of
interest is the expected signature of the changing split, not evidence of a defective mesh study.

signature.
4. Grid Convergence Index (GCI)
The Roache/Richardson grid convergence index is the firm's verification instrument for RANS and steady work only.
GCI is not valid for LES and shall not be used to verify any large-eddy result issued from this firm.
The reason is physical. Under systematic mesh refinement, an LES does not converge to a unique grid-independent
solution. As the filter width narrows, energy migrates from the modelled sub-grid-scale contribution into the explicitly
resolved field; the resolved-to-modelled turbulence split changes with the mesh. A three-grid sequence of LES

•

•

2. Definitions
Grid convergence index (GCI). A quantitative estimator of numerical uncertainty attributable to spatial discretisation
error, computed from a monotonic sequence of solutions on systematically refined grids under an assumed observed
order of accuracy. Reported as a percentage band on a selected integrated quantity of interest. The GCI is defined
for solutions that converge to a unique grid-independent limit as the mesh is refined.
Plume resolution index (D*/dx). The ratio of the characteristic plume diameter D* to the representative fire-region
cell edge length dx. D* is the buoyancy-driven length scale associated with a fire heat release rate Q_dot and is
defined as
D* = ( Q_dot / ( rho_inf · cp · T_inf · sqrt(g) ) )^{2/5}
where rho_inf, cp and T_inf are the ambient density, specific heat and absolute temperature respectively, and g is
gravitational acceleration. The index D*/dx is the standard measure of how many cells span the buoyancy-dominated
length scale of a fire plume.
Resolved turbulent kinetic energy (k_res). The turbulent kinetic energy carried by the explicitly resolved velocity
fluctuations in a large-eddy simulation, distinct from the sub-grid-scale contribution k_sgs modelled by the closure.
The resolved fraction is defined as k_res / (k_res + k_sgs).

simulations run to steady state, whether solved with a pseudo-time or true-steady solver, including internal buoyant

4. Grid Convergence Index (GCI)
The Roache/Richardson grid convergence index is the firm's verification instrument for RANS and steady work only.
GCI is not valid for LES and shall not be used to verify any large-eddy result issued from this firm.
The reason is physical. Under systematic mesh refinement, an LES does not converge to a unique grid-independent
solution. As the filter width narrows, energy migrates from the modelled sub-grid-scale contribution into the explicitly
resolved field; the resolved-to-modelled turbulence split changes with the mesh. A three-grid sequence of LES
solutions therefore records a change in the physical content of the simulation between grids rather than a
discretisation-error tail collapsing toward a limit. The Richardson extrapolation on which the GCI is built assumes that
limit exists. It does not exist for LES, and therefore GCI values computed from an LES three-grid study are
numerically well-formed but physically meaningless. Non-monotonic behaviour in an LES three-grid quantity of
interest is the expected signature of the changing split, not evidence of a defective mesh study.

refined grids with representative cell sizes h_1 < h_2 < h_3, refinement ratios r_21 = h_2 / h_1 and r_32 = h_3 / h_2
each at least 1.3, and a scalar quantity of interest phi with values phi_1, phi_2, phi_3 on the three grids, the observed
order of accuracy p is obtained from

solved for p by fixed-point iteration. The fine-grid GCI on the finest pair is then
GCI_fine = F_s · | ( phi_2 − phi_1 ) / phi_1 | / ( r_21^p − 1 )
with a safety factor F_s of 1.25 when three or more grids are used. Reported GCI values shall carry the safety factor
and the observed p, and shall state the quantity of interest to which they apply. Monotonic convergence is a
precondition for reporting a GCI; oscillatory or divergent triples shall be flagged and the mesh study extended rather
than reported as a GCI band.

solve without a reported GCI (or an equivalent Roache/Richardson estimator) is not accepted.

THE CFD ME | Tucson, Arizona | Units and Conversions SOP | rev 2 | Effective 04/01/2025
Document: Units and Conversions Standard Operating Procedure Revision: rev 2 Effective Date: 04/01/2025
Author / Owner: Marguerite Falk, PE — Technical Director & Reviewing Engineer (AZ PE #42798) Applies to: All
engineering analyses, hand calculations, CFD case files, review checklists, memos, and reports produced by The
CFD Mechanical Engineer, LLC. Supersedes: Units and Conversions SOP rev 1.
1. Scope and General Principles
This procedure governs the units in which engineering quantities are computed, recorded, exchanged, and reported
at The CFD ME. It applies to every analyst and reviewer inside the firm, to every contracted CFD hour executed by
third parties on our behalf, and to every artifact — case files, logs, hand-calc worksheets, memos, and client
deliverables — that leaves any engineer's workstation.
The governing principles are three:
SI units shall be used internally throughout all analyses. Reports transmitted to clients working in US customary units
shall include a conversion table in report Section 1. Every numeric value in every artifact shall carry its unit in the
same cell or sentence — a bare number without unit is a defect.
The three principles are jointly binding. Internal SI discipline is not satisfied by a conversion applied at report time; it is
satisfied by keeping the analysis in SI from mesh generation through post-processing so that reviewers see a single
coherent unit system when they audit a case. The conversion table is not optional decoration; on projects whose
client-facing basis is US customary (ASCE 7 wind loads, ASHRAE inputs, Red Butte lab reports quoted in inches and
pounds), the table in Section 1 is the artifact the client uses to cross-read our numbers against their own, and its
absence is grounds for rejection at peer review. The unit-in-the-same-cell rule applies to spreadsheets, CSV column
headers, plot axis labels, memo text, and inline references — no exception is made for "obvious" units or for context
inherited from a section heading.
2. Preferred Units by Quantity
The following preferred units apply to all internal work. Deviations require written justification in the case-setup memo
and reviewer sign-off.
